title: Local publishers and publishing The Full Moon Rag in 1909
summary: Carew recalls Williams and Pirone, other New Orleans publishers, and getting The Full Moon Rag published by Pewter in 1909.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: close to that is that at the corner Canal and Rampart Street there used to be a small open truck, one of these light delivery trucks with an open wagon. And they had a couple of pieces of music in that, and a Negro standing in the back or sitting in the back singing. They used to give a little concert there on the street like that, but it wasn't like a street singer really. It wasn't Clarence Williams and Pirone trying to sell their music for us. No, I never saw them. The messenger at the Custom House when I was working there in the 1916-17 would occasionally bring me in a piece of music that Williams and Pirone published. He lived, he was a neighbor of theirs out there. He'd bring it into me in the Custom House, music they published a little bit. Well, they must have been one of the early publishers. As far as that type of music goes, there were. Not that type of Negro music. There were, there was any music store in town, now and then would put out a piece of music. They'd have somebody get enthusiastic, you know, or compose a piece and come in and convince them that it would be a good thing to publish. And they would put it out. And, as I say, any, any store in town. Now, this Baby Seals, he had one piece published by Groove Wall there in New Orleans that was called Shake, Rattle and Roll. And you got to shake, rattle and roll or my money ain't wine. And the fellow by the name of Karoo got into D. H. Holmes and tried to persuade them to publish a piece, but the man says he wasn't publishing anything then. He carried, he carried me around to John Pewter and Pewter published my piece for me. So, that's the answer. What was that? The title of it? The title was The Full Moon Rag, or The Full Moon. And so Pewter put it out. He was very... What year was that? In 1909. Oh, yes. Would you like to see the cover?
Well, I have seen the cover. Have you? Yes. Someone in Chicago has a copy of it, and I think I've seen your... Is that Mr. Hardin or someone by the name? Yes, yes. You know him? Yes.

Well, I know he had it because he gave one to Jerry Heerman's. I believe he did at least. Yes, that was 1909. It would have been 1908, but he said, Well, here, it's pretty near the end of the year. Let's get a very good, fresh date on it. We wait after the first of the year. So, he published that. How many tunes have you had published? That's all. That one? Did you renew it a few years ago? No, I didn't. See? That showed how little I was thinking of that until Jetty Roll came to town. You did? I wrote to the library, not to renew it, but I wrote to ask them if I could have the copies that were deposited there, because I'd run out of them. And they never replied to my letter, but they just sent back my letter with the copyright date on it, just mailed it back to me. Maybe not taking time to read your letter and really understand it. Well, they wouldn't have published it. There's a strange thing about that. They wouldn't at that time have printed it for me, or given it to me. They leave the copies there as owned by the man that publishes them. Oh. Pewter could have gotten them. Oh, that's not. But I couldn't. Even after they expired. I think that you can get photocopies. Oh, yes, I did. I finally did. I gave all I had away, and then I didn't have any myself, so I got photocopies of it afterwards. Has anyone ever recorded it? No, I don't think so. No, I'm sure they haven't. Or is that good?
